tool.name: VS Code
tool.tagline: Extensible code editor with built-in Git, terminal and debugger
tool.description: Visual Studio Code is a free, cross-platform code editor from Microsoft with IntelliSense, an integrated terminal, Git support and a debugger, extended by a huge marketplace of language and tool extensions. It is the most widely used editor among developers, and knowing it well removes a lot of daily friction.

glossary.def: In VS Code, the folder (or set of folders) you have opened. Search, Git, tasks and workspace settings all apply to it.
The column of icons on the far left of VS Code that switches the side bar between Explorer, Search, Source Control, Extensions and other views.
The area next to VS Code's activity bar that shows the chosen view, such as the file tree. Ctrl+B hides or shows it.
One section of VS Code's editor area with its own tabs; splitting the editor puts groups side by side.
The strip along the bottom of the VS Code window showing the Git branch, problems, cursor position and file language; its items can be clicked.
VS Code's way of opening a single-clicked file in a temporary tab (title in italics) that the next clicked file replaces.
VS Code's searchable list of every command, opened with Ctrl+Shift+P (or F1).
VS Code's Ctrl+P box for opening files by a few letters of their name; starting characters like @, # or : switch it to symbols or line numbers.
An add-on for VS Code, installed from its Marketplace, that adds support for a language, a tool, a theme or new commands.
A named piece of code, such as a function, a class or a variable, that an editor can list, jump to and rename.
Several blinking text cursors at once in VS Code, so whatever you type appears in every one of those places.
VS Code's suggestions while you type: possible next names, with short explanations, worked out by a language server.
A helper program that understands one programming language and tells the editor about the code: suggestions, errors, definitions and safe renames.
The bar above VS Code's editor showing the path to where you are: folders, file, then the symbol the cursor is in. Each part can be clicked.
VS Code's understanding of what happens in its terminal: where each command starts, whether it succeeded, and where its output is.
A VS Code task setting that reads a tool's output and turns its error lines into clickable entries in the Problems panel.
A breakpoint-like marker in VS Code that prints a message when a line runs, without pausing the program or changing its code.
A small program that connects VS Code's debugging screen to the debugger of one particular language.
A condition on a VS Code keyboard shortcut, such as editorTextFocus, saying where the shortcut applies.
A reusable piece of text or code you insert by typing a short prefix, with spots you fill in by pressing Tab.
A numbered spot inside a snippet ($1, $2...) where the cursor goes next when you press Tab.
VS Code's feature that keeps settings, extensions and shortcuts the same on all your computers, by signing in with GitHub or Microsoft.
The back half of VS Code, installed on a remote machine or container, that reads files, runs terminals and runs extensions there while the window stays on your computer.
A container described by a devcontainer.json file that holds a project's complete set of tools, so VS Code can open the project inside it.
A framework for building desktop apps with web technologies; VS Code is built on it.
The separate background program in which VS Code runs all extensions, so a slow extension can't freeze typing.
The trigger that makes VS Code load an extension, such as opening a Python file or running one of its commands.
An open standard for how editors and language servers talk, so one language server can power many editors.
An open standard for how editors talk to debug adapters, so one debugging screen can work with many languages.
A second VS Code window, started with F5 from an extension project, that runs the extension you are writing so you can try and debug it.

concepts.name: The interface and opening folders
concepts.summary: Open a project folder, and find your way around the five areas of VS Code's window.
concepts.why: Knowing where everything lives makes the rest of VS Code discoverable instead of overwhelming.
concepts.body:
VS Code is a code editor: a text editor built for the files of programming projects, with colours that make code easier to read, a built-in terminal, Git support and much more. It is free, made by Microsoft, and runs on Windows, macOS and Linux.

It works best when you open a whole project **folder**, not single files: `File > Open Folder`. The open folder is called your **workspace**, and search, Git and settings all apply to it.

You can also open it from a terminal: `code .` opens the folder you are in (the dot means "this folder"). On Windows and Linux the installer sets up the `code` command; on macOS, open the Command Palette (next lesson) and run `Shell Command: Install 'code' command in PATH` once.

The window has five areas. On the far left, the **activity bar** is a strip of icons: Explorer (your files), Search, Source Control (Git), Extensions (add-ons) and more. Clicking one changes what the **side bar** next to it shows, such as your file tree; `Ctrl+B` hides or shows the side bar.

The big middle area is the **editor**, holding your open files as tabs. It can be split into side-by-side **editor groups** with `Ctrl+\`. Below it, the **panel** holds the Terminal, the list of Problems and other output; `Ctrl+J` hides or shows it.

Along the bottom, the **status bar** shows your Git branch, how many errors and warnings were found, the cursor's line number and position, and the file's language. Each item can be clicked to change it.

Shortcuts in this course use Windows and Linux keys; on macOS, press `Cmd` where it says `Ctrl` in most of them.

Single-clicking a file opens it in **preview mode**: its tab title is in italics, and the next file you click replaces it. Double-click the file, or start typing in it, to keep it open. `Ctrl+Tab` switches between open files.
concepts.code:
# from a terminal
code .                      # open the current folder as a workspace
code -g src/app.ts:42       # open a file at line 42 (-g = go to)
code --diff old.json new.json   # compare two files side by side
code --new-window ~/notes   # open another folder in a new window

# inside VS Code
#   Ctrl+B        side bar on/off        Ctrl+J   panel on/off
#   Ctrl+\        split the editor       Ctrl+Tab switch open files
#   Ctrl+Shift+E  Explorer               Ctrl+Shift+X  Extensions
takeaways: Open folders (code .), not loose files
Activity bar picks the side bar view; Ctrl+B and Ctrl+J toggle side bar and panel
Italic tab = preview; double-click to keep it open
pitfalls: Opening a parent folder that holds many projects; Git, search and settings then work on the wrong folder.

quiz.q: Why does a file you single-clicked disappear when you click another file?
options: It was closed due to an error
VS Code limits open tabs to one
It opened in preview mode, which reuses the tab
quiz.explain: Preview tabs (italic title) are replaced by the next preview until you edit or double-click them.

concepts.name: Command Palette and Quick Open
concepts.summary: Ctrl+Shift+P runs any command by name; Ctrl+P opens files from a few letters of their name, and a first character like @, : or > changes what it searches.
concepts.why: Every feature is reachable from the palette, so you never need to memorise menus.
concepts.body:
The **Command Palette** (`Ctrl+Shift+P`, or `F1`) lists every command that VS Code and its add-ons, called **extensions** (covered later), provide. Type a few letters, such as "sort lines", "toggle word wrap" or "reload window", and press Enter. The palette shows each command's keyboard shortcut next to it, so it doubles as a way to learn shortcuts.

**Quick Open** (`Ctrl+P`) finds files in your workspace from a few letters of their name, even with letters skipped: `usrctl` finds `UserController.ts`. What you type first changes what it does:

- `>` turns it into the Command Palette.
- `:` goes to a line number (`:120`), same as `Ctrl+G`.
- `?` shows all available prefixes.

Two more prefixes work with **symbols**: the named pieces inside a code file. A common kind is a **function**, a named set of instructions the program can run again and again, like `calculateTotal`.

- `@` lists the symbols in the current file, such as functions and classes (a **class** is a named blueprint for one kind of thing in a program, like `Customer`); `@:` groups them by kind.
- `#` searches symbols across the whole workspace.

Press `Ctrl+P` repeatedly to cycle through recently opened files.

The full shortcut list is under `File > Preferences > Keyboard Shortcuts` (`Ctrl+K Ctrl+S`), where you can search by command name or by pressing the keys themselves. If you come from another editor, "keymap" extensions (Vim, Sublime, IntelliJ...) change the shortcuts to the ones your fingers already know.
concepts.code:
# Ctrl+Shift+P  then type:
#   >Sort Lines Ascending
#   >Developer: Reload Window
#   >View: Toggle Word Wrap
# Ctrl+P  then type:
#   usrctl            matches UserController.ts
#   @render           jump to the symbol 'render' in this file
#   #parseConfig      a symbol anywhere in the workspace
#   :120              go to line 120
# Ctrl+K Ctrl+S     open the Keyboard Shortcuts editor
takeaways: Ctrl+Shift+P runs any command and shows its shortcut
Ctrl+P opens files; @ symbols in this file, # in the workspace, : a line
Ctrl+K Ctrl+S searches and edits keyboard shortcuts

quiz.q: In Quick Open (Ctrl+P), what does typing `@` first do?
options: Lists symbols in the current file
quiz.explain: The @ prefix switches Quick Open to listing the symbols (functions, classes and so on) in the open file.

concepts.name: Multi-cursor editing and IntelliSense
concepts.summary: Type in several places at once with multiple cursors, move and copy lines, comment and format code, and let IntelliSense suggest what comes next.
concepts.why: These few shortcuts cover most day-to-day editing and save hundreds of keystrokes a day.
concepts.body:
**Multiple cursors** let you type in several places at once:

- `Alt+Click` (Option+Click on macOS) adds a cursor where you click.
- `Ctrl+D` selects the next place the current word appears, with a cursor there too; repeat to add more, and `Ctrl+K Ctrl+D` skips one.
- `Ctrl+Shift+L` selects **every** place it appears.
- `Ctrl+Alt+Up/Down` (Option+Cmd+Up/Down on macOS) adds cursors on the lines above or below; `Shift+Alt` plus dragging selects a rectangular block.

**Line operations**: `Alt+Up/Down` moves the current line, `Shift+Alt+Up/Down` copies it, `Ctrl+Shift+K` deletes it, `Ctrl+Enter` inserts a line below, and `Ctrl+/` turns the line into a comment (a note for people that the program ignores) and back.

**IntelliSense** is VS Code's name for suggestions as you type: names that could come next, with short explanations. It relies on a **language server**, a helper program that understands the file's programming language, usually installed with an extension for that language (Pylance for Python, for example). `Ctrl+Space` asks for suggestions; `Ctrl+Shift+Space` shows what a function expects to be given.

**Quick fixes**: when VS Code spots a problem it knows how to repair, a light bulb appears. Click it, or press `Ctrl+.`, to pick a fix, such as adding a missing line that brings in code from another file.

`F2` renames a symbol everywhere it is used, across files, touching only real uses, unlike find-and-replace. `Shift+Alt+F` (`Ctrl+Shift+I` on Linux) tidies the file's spacing and layout into a standard style, using the **formatter** set up for that language.

Use `Ctrl+D` for "change this name here and in the next few places", and `F2` when you want every use in the whole project.
concepts.code:
# rename three occurrences of 'item' to 'product':
#   double-click 'item', Ctrl+D, Ctrl+D, then type 'product'
# add a semicolon to the end of 5 lines:
#   Ctrl+Alt+Down x4, End, type ';'
# Alt+Up / Alt+Down          move line
# Shift+Alt+Down             copy line below
# Ctrl+/                     comment / uncomment line
# Ctrl+Space                 ask for suggestions
# Ctrl+.                     quick fix
# F2                         rename symbol everywhere
# Shift+Alt+F                format the file
takeaways: Ctrl+D adds the next match; Ctrl+Shift+L selects all of them
Alt+Up/Down moves lines, Ctrl+/ comments them
F2 renames safely across files; Ctrl+. shows quick fixes
pitfalls: Using Ctrl+Shift+L or find-and-replace to rename something in code; it also changes unrelated text that happens to match. Use F2.

quiz.q: You want to rename a function and update every place that uses it across the project. Which is safest?
options: Search and replace in all files
quiz.explain: Rename Symbol asks the language server, so it changes only real uses of that function, in every file.

concepts.name: Search and code navigation
concepts.summary: Search across all files with filters and patterns, and jump through code: to where something is defined, to where it is used, and back again.
concepts.why: Reading and understanding code is mostly navigation; doing it by keyboard keeps you in flow.
concepts.body:
**Search across files** with `Ctrl+Shift+F`. Toggles in the search box match upper and lower case exactly, match whole words only, or treat your text as a **regular expression** (regex): a mini-language for text patterns, where `TODO|FIXME` means "either word".

The "..." button reveals **files to include** and **files to exclude**, written as **glob patterns**: wildcards for file names, where `*` matches any characters within a name and `**` any number of folders. So `src/**/*.ts` means every `.ts` file anywhere under `src`. Files listed in `.gitignore` are skipped by default.

`Ctrl+Shift+H` replaces across files, showing each change as a diff before you apply it. With regex on, `$1` in the replacement puts back whatever matched the first bracketed part of the pattern.

In code, every symbol is **defined** in one place (where it is created) and used in others. With help from a language server (a helper program that understands the file's language), VS Code jumps between them:

- `F12` goes to the definition; `Ctrl+Click` does the same with the mouse.
- `Alt+F12` **peeks**: it shows the definition in a small window right where you are.
- `Shift+F12` lists every place the symbol is used; `Shift+Alt+F12` shows them in a side view.
- `Ctrl+Shift+O` jumps to a symbol in this file, `Ctrl+T` to one anywhere in the workspace.
- `F8` jumps to the next error or warning.

After jumping, `Alt+Left` on Windows (`Ctrl+-` on macOS, `Ctrl+Alt+-` on Linux) goes back to where you were, and the matching forward shortcut returns, like the Back and Forward buttons of a web **browser**. The **breadcrumbs** bar above the editor shows where you are: the folders and file, then the symbol you are inside. Click any part to jump to its neighbours.

`Ctrl+F` and `Ctrl+H` are find and replace in the current file, with the same regex option.
concepts.code:
# Ctrl+Shift+F   search in files
#   query:       TODO|FIXME          (regex enabled)
#   include:     src/**/*.ts
#   exclude:     **/*.test.ts
# Ctrl+Shift+H   replace in files
#   find:        console\.log\((.*)\)
#   replace:     logger.debug($1)
# F12            go to definition     Alt+F12   peek definition
# Shift+F12      find references      Ctrl+T    workspace symbol
# Alt+Left       navigate back        F8        next problem
takeaways: Ctrl+Shift+F searches all files, with regex and include/exclude patterns
F12 definition, Alt+F12 peek, Shift+F12 every use
Go back after a jump; F8 cycles through problems
pitfalls: Wondering why a file is missing from search results; it may be excluded by .gitignore or search.exclude.

quiz.q: Which shortcut shows a definition inline without leaving the current file?
quiz.explain: Alt+F12 opens Peek Definition in an embedded view.

concepts.name: Git in VS Code
concepts.summary: Stage, commit, compare, switch branches, push, pull and resolve merge conflicts from the Source Control view, using the Git you already know.
concepts.why: Reviewing diffs and staging parts of files visually is faster and less error-prone than doing everything in the terminal.
concepts.body:
VS Code's **Source Control** view (`Ctrl+Shift+G`) is a visual layer over the `git` installed on your machine; behind the scenes it runs the same commands you know.

- **Changes** lists modified files; clicking one opens a **diff editor** (left = HEAD or the staging area, right = working tree).
- The `+` icon stages a file (`git add`). In the diff editor you can stage or revert individual **ranges** via the gutter or by selecting lines and running "Stage Selected Ranges" , the point-and-click version of `git add -p`.
- Type a message and press `Ctrl+Enter` to commit what is staged.
- The status bar shows the current **branch** (click to switch or create one) and a `Sync Changes` button that pulls, then pushes.
- The editor gutter shows coloured bars for added, modified and deleted lines; click one to see the change inline.

**Merge conflicts** open with inline "Accept Current / Accept Incoming / Accept Both" actions, and a three-way **merge editor** shows yours, theirs and the result side by side. After resolving, stage the file and commit as usual.

The **Timeline** view in the Explorer shows a file's commit history, and "Open Changes" on a commit diffs it. Popular extensions such as GitLens add blame annotations and richer history.

Whatever you click, the Git output is logged: open the Output panel and choose "Git" to see the exact commands VS Code ran, a great way to learn, and to work out what went wrong.
concepts.code:
# Ctrl+Shift+G         open Source Control
# click file           diff editor: HEAD/index vs working tree
# +                    stage file          (git add file)
# select lines > right-click > Stage Selected Ranges   (like git add -p)
# message + Ctrl+Enter commit staged       (git commit -m)
# status bar branch    switch/create branch (git switch / -c)
# sync button          git pull then git push
# Output panel > Git   shows the real commands, e.g.
#   > git add -A -- /home/ann/shop/src/cart.ts
#   > git commit --quiet --allow-empty-message --file -
takeaways: Source Control is a visual layer over your local git
Stage files or selected ranges, Ctrl+Enter to commit
Output > Git shows the exact git commands run
pitfalls: Pressing `Sync Changes` without checking what it will send and fetch; it runs pull and push together.

quiz.q: How do you stage only some changed lines of a file in VS Code?
options: Select them in the diff editor and use Stage Selected Ranges
quiz.explain: Staging selected ranges puts just those lines into the staging area, like git add -p.

concepts.name: The integrated terminal
concepts.summary: Open terminals inside VS Code with Ctrl+`, split and name them, choose which shell they run, and use shell integration features.
concepts.why: Keeping the terminal next to your code avoids window switching and lets VS Code link errors back to files.
concepts.body:
`` Ctrl+` `` toggles the **integrated terminal** in the panel; it starts in the workspace folder and runs your default **shell**, the program that reads and carries out the commands you type. `` Ctrl+Shift+` `` opens another one.

- Several terminals appear as tabs on the right of the panel; you can **split** one (`Ctrl+Shift+5`) to see two side by side, and rename or colour them.
- The dropdown next to `+` chooses a **profile**: bash, zsh, PowerShell, Git Bash, or Linux inside Windows through WSL... Set the default with the `terminal.integrated.defaultProfile.<os>` setting.
- Terminals can be dragged into the editor area or moved to a separate window.

**Shell integration** (on by default for bash, zsh, fish and PowerShell) lets VS Code understand commands: decorations mark each command as succeeded or failed, `Ctrl+Up/Down` jumps between commands, and the "Run Recent Command" picker (`Ctrl+Alt+R`) searches history across sessions.

**Links**: file paths with line numbers in output (`src/app.ts:42:7`) and URLs are clickable with `Ctrl+Click`, which is how test failures take you straight to the line.

To send code to a terminal, select it and run "Terminal: Run Selected Text In Active Terminal". Language extensions often add their own, such as running the current Python file. Note that the integrated terminal gets its environment settings from VS Code itself, as they were when VS Code started. If you change `PATH` (the list of folders the shell searches for programs) in your shell's start-up file, restart VS Code, not just the terminal.
concepts.code:
# Ctrl+`             toggle terminal panel
# Ctrl+Shift+`       new terminal
# Ctrl+Shift+5       split terminal
# Ctrl+Up / Ctrl+Down   jump between previous commands (shell integration)
# Ctrl+Alt+R         run recent command
# Ctrl+Click         open file:line or URL from the output
// settings.json
{
  "terminal.integrated.defaultProfile.linux": "zsh",
  "terminal.integrated.scrollback": 10000
}
takeaways: Ctrl+` toggles; terminals can be split, named and moved
Profiles choose the shell; set a default per OS
Shell integration adds command navigation and clickable paths
pitfalls: Updating PATH in your shell profile and expecting the existing VS Code window to see it; restart VS Code.

quiz.q: Clicking `src/app.ts:42:7` in terminal output with Ctrl does what?
options: Nothing; links only work for URLs
quiz.explain: The terminal detects file paths with positions and opens them in the editor.

concepts.name: User and workspace settings
concepts.summary: Configure VS Code in the Settings editor or settings.json, for yourself or for one project, with rules for individual languages.
concepts.why: Settings like format-on-save and per-project rules make the editor do the right thing automatically for every teammate.
concepts.body:
Open settings with `Ctrl+,`. The Settings editor is searchable; the `{}` icon in the top right opens the underlying **settings.json**, which is what most people edit directly.

Settings exist at several levels, the more specific winning:

- **User** settings apply to every window.
- **Workspace** settings live in `.vscode/settings.json` inside the project and override user settings. Commit them to share project conventions with the team (formatter, tab size, excluded folders).
- **Language-specific** blocks override both for one language: `"[python]": { "editor.tabSize": 4 }`.
- In a multi-root workspace, folder settings are also possible.

Useful settings to know:

- `"editor.formatOnSave": true` plus `"editor.defaultFormatter"` per language.
- `"editor.codeActionsOnSave"` to run automatic fixes on save, such as sorting the lines that load other files, or fixes suggested by a linter like ESLint.
- `"files.exclude"` hides files from the Explorer; `"search.exclude"` from search.
- `"files.autoSave": "afterDelay"` saves automatically.

settings.json is written in **JSON**, a common text format for settings and data, here with comments allowed (jsonc), and IntelliSense completes setting names and values. Hovering a setting shows its description and default. Search for `@modified` in the Settings UI to see everything you changed from defaults.
takeaways: User < Workspace (.vscode/settings.json) < language-specific
Commit workspace settings to share project conventions
settings.json is JSON with comments; @modified shows changes
pitfalls: Putting personal preferences like themes or font size in the shared workspace settings.

quiz.q: A user setting sets tabSize 2, the workspace sets 4, and a [python] block in the workspace sets 8. What is the tab size in a Python file?
quiz.explain: Language-specific settings override general ones, and workspace overrides user.

concepts.name: Extensions and recommendations
concepts.summary: Install language support, linters and tools from the Marketplace, manage them per workspace and recommend them to your team.
concepts.why: Most of VS Code's power comes from extensions; choosing and managing them well keeps it fast and consistent.
concepts.body:
Open the **Extensions** view with `Ctrl+Shift+X`. Each extension has an ID in the form `publisher.name`, such as `ms-python.python` or `dbaeumer.vscode-eslint`. Prefer verified publishers and widely used extensions; an extension runs code with your user's permissions.

What to install typically:

- **Language support**: VS Code understands many languages a little out of the box, but rich suggestions, debugging and testing come from extensions (Python, Go, Rust Analyzer, C#, Java...). Most run a **language server**, a helper program that understands the language, in the background.
- **Linters and formatters**: ESLint, Prettier, Ruff...
- **Tools**: Docker, remote development, GitLens, and tools for trying out web services.

Managing them:

- Disable an extension **for a workspace** when a project does not need it; fewer active extensions means faster startup.
- From a terminal: `code --install-extension ms-python.python`, `code --list-extensions`.
- `.vscode/extensions.json` with a `"recommendations"` list makes VS Code prompt teammates to install the project's extensions, a lightweight way to standardise tooling.

Extensions contribute commands (search "ExtensionName:" in the palette), settings (filter the Settings editor by `@ext:publisher.name`) and keybindings. If something misbehaves, "Help: Start Extension Bisect" finds the culprit by turning off half of the extensions at a time and asking whether the problem is still there.
concepts.code:
code --install-extension ms-python.python
code --install-extension dbaeumer.vscode-eslint
code --list-extensions --show-versions | head -3
# dbaeumer.vscode-eslint@<version>
# ms-python.python@<version>
# ...
# .vscode/extensions.json  (prompt teammates to install these)
cat > .vscode/extensions.json <<'EOF'
{
  "recommendations": ["ms-python.python", "charliermarsh.ruff"],
  "unwantedRecommendations": ["ms-python.autopep8"]
}
EOF
takeaways: Extension IDs are publisher.name; install from the view or with code --install-extension
.vscode/extensions.json recommends extensions to the team
Disable per workspace; Extension Bisect finds a misbehaving one
pitfalls: Installing dozens of overlapping extensions (several formatters for one language) that fight each other.

quiz.q: How do you prompt everyone opening a repo to install the project's linter extension?
quiz.explain: VS Code reads .vscode/extensions.json and offers to install the recommended extensions.

concepts.name: Debugging with breakpoints and launch.json
concepts.summary: Start the debugger with F5, set breakpoints, logpoints and conditions, inspect variables, and configure launches in launch.json.
concepts.why: A real debugger finds bugs far faster than print statements, and VS Code makes it available for almost every language.
concepts.body:
VS Code's debugger is generic; language extensions provide **debug adapters** (Node.js is built in, Python via the Python extension, and so on).

Basics: click left of a line number or press `F9` to set a **breakpoint**, then `F5` to start. When execution stops you get:

- **Variables** and **Watch** panels, plus hovering over any variable in the editor.
- The **Call Stack**: the chain of functions that called each other to reach this line; click one to see its variables.
- The **Debug Console**, where you can evaluate expressions in the paused context.
- Controls: `F5` continue, `F10` step over, `F11` step into, `Shift+F11` step out, `Shift+F5` stop.

Right-click the gutter for smarter breakpoints:

- **Conditional** breakpoints stop only when an expression is true (`order.total > 1000`), or after a **hit count**.
- **Logpoints** print a message with `{expressions}` without stopping or editing code, ideal when pausing would disturb what you are watching.

For anything beyond "run this file", create `.vscode/launch.json` (Run and Debug view > "create a launch.json file"). Each configuration has a `type` (debugger), a `request` (`launch` starts a program, `attach` connects to one already running, such as a server in a container), and options like `program`, `args`, `env` and `cwd`. Variables such as `${workspaceFolder}` and `${file}` keep it portable. `preLaunchTask` can run a build first.
takeaways: F9 breakpoint, F5 start/continue, F10 over, F11 into
Conditional breakpoints and logpoints avoid code edits
launch.json: type, request (launch/attach), program, args, env
pitfalls: Leaving debug-only code edits (prints, sleeps) in place when a logpoint would have done the job.

quiz.q: You want to log a value every time a line runs, without pausing or changing the code. Use:
quiz.explain: Logpoints print a message with interpolated expressions and continue execution.

concepts.name: Tasks and problem matchers
concepts.summary: Define build, test and lint commands in tasks.json, run them with shortcuts and turn their output into clickable problems.
concepts.why: Tasks give every project one-key build and test commands and integrate tool errors into the Problems panel.
concepts.body:
A **task** is a named command VS Code can run for you. Many are auto-detected (npm scripts, Make, Gulp...); run any with "Tasks: Run Task".

Custom tasks live in `.vscode/tasks.json`:

- `label` names it; `type: "shell"` runs `command` in a shell; `"process"` runs a program directly.
- `group` marks it as the default **build** task (`Ctrl+Shift+B`) or **test** task.
- `dependsOn` chains tasks, with `dependsOrder: "sequence"` to run them in order.
- `presentation` controls the terminal: reuse, focus, clear.
- `options.cwd` and `options.env` set directory and environment.

**Problem matchers** parse the task output and turn errors into entries in the Problems panel with clickable locations. Built-in ones include `$tsc`, `$eslint-stylish`, `$gcc` and `$go`; you can also define a regex-based matcher. For long-running watch tasks (`tsc --watch`, or a development web server that keeps running), set `isBackground: true` with a background matcher so VS Code knows when the task is "ready", which matters when another configuration uses it as `preLaunchTask`.

Tasks are also how debugging setups build before launching. Keep them in the repository so every developer gets the same commands, and prefer calling project scripts (`npm run build`) rather than duplicating logic in tasks.json.
takeaways: tasks.json defines labelled commands; Ctrl+Shift+B runs the default build
problemMatcher turns output into clickable Problems
isBackground + matcher for watch tasks used as preLaunchTask
pitfalls: A watch task used as preLaunchTask without isBackground, so the debugger waits forever for it to finish.

options: Parses tsc output into entries in the Problems panel
quiz.explain: Problem matchers turn compiler output lines into diagnostics with file locations.

concepts.name: Keybindings, snippets and profiles
concepts.summary: Rebind keys with when clauses in keybindings.json, write your own snippets with tab stops, and switch setups with profiles and Settings Sync.
concepts.why: Tailoring shortcuts and repetitive code to your workflow, and keeping it the same on every machine, is where heavy users gain most.
concepts.body:
**Keybindings.** The Keyboard Shortcuts editor (`Ctrl+K Ctrl+S`) edits `keybindings.json`, a list of rules with `key`, `command`, optional `args` and a **when clause**: a condition on where you are, such as `editorTextFocus`, `terminalFocus` or `editorLangId == 'markdown'`. The same key can do different things in different contexts. Prefix a command with `-` to remove a default binding. "Developer: Toggle Keyboard Shortcuts Troubleshooting" logs which rule fired for each key press.

**Snippets.** "Snippets: Configure Snippets" creates global or per-language snippet files. Each snippet has a `prefix` (what you type), a `body` and an optional description. In the body:

- `$1`, `$2` are **tab stops**, `$0` the final cursor position.
- `${1:default}` is a placeholder; repeating `$1` mirrors the text.
- Variables like `$TM_FILENAME_BASE`, `$CURRENT_YEAR` and `$CLIPBOARD` insert context.

Project snippets can live in `.vscode/*.code-snippets` and are shared via the repo.

**Profiles** bundle settings, extensions, keybindings, snippets and UI state. Create one per context (say, "Python data", "Writing", "Presentation" with big fonts) and switch instantly; a folder can remember its profile. **Settings Sync** (sign in with GitHub or Microsoft) keeps profiles and settings identical across your machines.
takeaways: keybindings.json rules: key, command, when; -command removes a default
Snippet bodies use $1 tab stops, ${1:placeholder}, $0 and variables
Profiles switch whole setups; Settings Sync shares them across machines
pitfalls: Adding a new binding for a key already used in that context without a when clause, silently breaking a default.

quiz.q: In a snippet body, what does writing `$1` twice do?
options: Mirrors the same text at both places as you type
quiz.explain: Repeated tab stop numbers are linked, so typing at one updates the other.

concepts.name: Remote development: SSH, containers, WSL
concepts.summary: Run VS Code's back half on a server, in a container or in WSL while the window stays local, and define repeatable setups with devcontainer.json.
concepts.why: Remote development gives you local-feeling editing on the machine where code actually runs, and reproducible environments for teams.
concepts.body:
VS Code is split into a **UI** (the window) and a **backend** that does file access, terminals, language servers and debugging. The Remote extensions move the backend elsewhere by installing a **VS Code Server** there:

- **Remote - SSH**: connect to any SSH host from your `~/.ssh/config`; files, terminals and extensions run on the server.
- **Dev Containers**: open a folder inside a Docker container defined by `.devcontainer/devcontainer.json`.
- **WSL**: develop inside a Linux distribution on Windows.
- **Remote Tunnels** (`code tunnel` on the remote machine) work without SSH access, through a Microsoft-relayed tunnel, and also from vscode.dev in a browser.

Extensions have a **kind**: UI extensions (themes, keymaps) stay local, while workspace extensions (language servers, linters, debuggers) must be installed on the remote side, which VS Code does per machine or container. When a program on the remote machine starts listening on a port, VS Code **forwards** it, so you can open it on your own computer.

A **devcontainer.json** makes the environment reproducible: base image or Dockerfile, **features** (prebuilt tool installs such as Node or the GitHub CLI), extensions and settings to install, `forwardPorts`, and lifecycle commands like `postCreateCommand`. Commit it and every developer, plus GitHub Codespaces, gets the same toolchain with "Reopen in Container".

When something breaks, the Output channel "Remote - SSH" or "Dev Containers" shows the server installation and connection log.
takeaways: The backend (VS Code Server) runs remotely; the UI stays local
Workspace extensions install on the remote side, UI extensions stay local
devcontainer.json defines a reproducible environment, also used by Codespaces
pitfalls: Installing a linter extension locally and wondering why it does nothing in a remote window; install it in the remote.

quiz.q: In a Remote - SSH window, where does a language server extension like Pylance run?
options: On the SSH host, in the VS Code Server's extension host
Nowhere; remote windows have no extensions
quiz.explain: Workspace extensions run next to the code, on the remote host.

concepts.name: Architecture: extension host, LSP and DAP
concepts.summary: VS Code runs extensions in a separate extension host process and talks to language servers and debuggers over open protocols.
concepts.why: Understanding the process model explains performance problems, crashes and why the same language servers work in many editors.
concepts.body:
VS Code is an **Electron** application. Electron is a toolkit that turns website code into a desktop app; it bundles Node.js, which lets that kind of code run on your computer like any other program.

In an Electron app a **main process** manages windows, and each window's **renderer** draws the workbench (the UI). Extensions do **not** run in the renderer. They run in a separate Node.js **extension host** process, so a slow or crashing extension cannot freeze typing; at worst the host restarts.

Remote and web setups add more extension hosts: one on the remote machine, and in the browser version of VS Code one inside a web worker, a helper that runs code in the background so the page stays responsive.

Extensions are loaded lazily via **activation events** (opening a Python file, running a command, a `workspaceContains` pattern). Badly configured extensions that activate on `*` slow startup for everyone.

Two open protocols do much of the heavy lifting:

- The **Language Server Protocol (LSP)**: a language server (often a separate process, such as Pyright, gopls or rust-analyzer) provides completion, diagnostics, go to definition and rename over JSON-RPC, a simple convention for sending requests and their replies as small JSON messages. The same servers power Neovim, Emacs and other editors.
- The **Debug Adapter Protocol (DAP)**: a debug adapter translates VS Code's generic debugging UI to a specific runtime's debugger.

Diagnosing problems:

- "Developer: Show Running Extensions" lists activation times and flags unresponsive extensions.
- "Developer: Startup Performance" breaks down window load time.
- `code --disable-extensions` starts clean; "Help: Start Extension Bisect" isolates a culprit.
- "Developer: Open Process Explorer" shows CPU and memory per process, including language servers.
concepts.code:
# start without extensions to test a problem
code --disable-extensions .
# show where time goes during startup
code --prof-startup .
# Command Palette:
#   Developer: Show Running Extensions   activation time per extension
#   Developer: Startup Performance       window load breakdown
#   Developer: Open Process Explorer     CPU/memory per process
#   Help: Start Extension Bisect         binary-search a bad extension
# Output panel > "Python Language Server" / "TypeScript": LSP logs
takeaways: Extensions run in an isolated extension host, not the UI process
Activation events load extensions lazily
LSP for language features, DAP for debuggers, shared with other editors
pitfalls: Blaming VS Code for slowness that comes from one extension; check Running Extensions first.

quiz.q: Why does a hung extension usually not freeze typing in the editor?
options: Extensions run in a separate extension host process
Extensions are limited to 1 second of CPU
Typing is handled by the language server
quiz.explain: The renderer handles input while extensions run in their own Node.js process.

concepts.name: Writing your own extension
concepts.summary: Scaffold an extension with yo code, contribute commands in package.json, use the vscode API in TypeScript and test it in the Extension Development Host.
concepts.why: A small custom extension can automate a team-specific workflow that no marketplace extension covers.
concepts.body:
Extensions are Node.js packages written in TypeScript or JavaScript. Create a starter project with the Yeoman project generator: `npx --package yo --package generator-code -- yo code`. It creates:

- `package.json` with the **manifest**: `engines.vscode` (minimum version), `main` (entry file), and a `contributes` section declaring commands, settings, keybindings, menus and more. Contributed commands activate the extension automatically when invoked.
- `src/extension.ts` exporting `activate(context)` and optionally `deactivate()`.

Inside `activate`, use the `vscode` API: `vscode.commands.registerCommand`, `vscode.window.activeTextEditor`, `vscode.window.showInformationMessage`, `vscode.workspace.getConfiguration`, and editing via `editor.edit` or `WorkspaceEdit`. Push every disposable (commands, listeners) into `context.subscriptions` so it is cleaned up on deactivation.

Press `F5` to launch an **Extension Development Host**, a second VS Code window with your extension loaded; breakpoints in your code work immediately. The generator also sets up tests run with `@vscode/test-cli`.

To share it, package with `npx @vscode/vsce package` (creates a `.vsix` you can install with `code --install-extension file.vsix`) or publish to the Marketplace under a publisher account. Keep activation narrow and work asynchronous; the extension host is shared with every other extension.
takeaways: package.json contributes declare commands, settings, menus
activate() registers handlers; push disposables to context.subscriptions
F5 opens an Extension Development Host; vsce packages a .vsix
pitfalls: Activating on every startup ("*") when a command or language activation event would do.

quiz.q: What does pressing F5 in a generated extension project do?
options: Opens an Extension Development Host window with your extension loaded for debugging
quiz.explain: The default launch configuration starts a second VS Code instance running your extension under the debugger.
